topic: Flood mitigation, drainage, and river-basin master-plan alignment
summary: Bivensio Dizon presented flood mitigation as a 2027 priority and said DPWH would shift toward basin-wide flood management, using major river-basin and LGU drainage master plans. He cited 83.84 billion in locally funded 2027 flood-mitigation projects and described ongoing dredging and desilting needs after more than twelve years without dredging major rivers. Representative Tobit Janko pressed for full publication of projects and allocations by legislative district, while Representative Dadah Kiram Ismula requested complete master-plan data and tables showing whether 2025–2027 projects aligned with those plans. DPWH's flood-mitigation director said the agency was updating plans for all 18 major river basins with catchment areas of 1,400 square kilometer and up, with climate-change updating every three years. Bivensio Dizon undertook to provide the requested alignment information and said a dredging and desilting plan was being prepared. A majority member also identified nationwide lump-sum items of 369,000,000 for dredging and waterway cleaning and 500,000,000 for drainage and flood-mitigation repairs, which DPWH said would be implemented based on need.
question: The committee sought to establish whether DPWH's flood-mitigation, drainage, dredging, and desilting projects were guided by current river-basin and local drainage master plans. It also sought the plans' status, the projects aligned with them, and how nationwide flood-mitigation lump-sum items would be allocated.
agency_position: DPWH said flood mitigation should be guided by major river-basin and LGU drainage master plans, with projects coordinated across national, regional, district, and local levels. The department said it was updating plans for all 18 major river basins, incorporating climate-change considerations, and allocating dredging, drainage, and other flood-mitigation works based on need, while relying in some cases on augmentation and savings.
outcome: DPWH answered the committee's questions in principle and undertook to submit master-plan data, project-alignment tables, district-level project information, and a dredging and desilting plan. The record did not show that the requested alignment tables or plan had been submitted during the hearing.

positions.position: Supported full transparency for flood-control and other DPWH projects, including publication by legislative district and line item, and questioned fragmented or unclear project phasing.

Sought complete and current master-plan data and project-by-project alignment tables to determine whether DPWH's proposed budget followed applicable regional, district, national, and river-basin plans.

Questioned how nationwide dredging, waterway-cleaning, drainage-repair, and flood-mitigation lump-sum appropriations would be implemented and expressed support for addressing the country's flooding problem.

Advocated basin-wide, coordinated flood mitigation; updating plans for climate change; completing unfinished projects; and using need-based, transparent implementation rather than disconnected projects.

topic: Project rationalization and DPWH absorptive capacity
summary: Bivensio Dizon said DPWH had reduced project numbers by eliminating duplicate and overlapping projects, removing projects below 5,000,000 pesos under the VIP program, and focusing on larger projects that implementing offices could absorb. He said DPWH had previously reached about 25,000 projects, compared with a typical average of 20,000, and that some offices had carried two to four times their ideal workload. The agency also reported that its 2026 capital outlay involved about 460 billion, with 15,032 projects advertised and 7,467 awarded as of 08/23/2026, and targeted 80% awards by the end of September. Representative Mike Tan asked whether DPWH had conservatively estimated implementing-office capacity and requested rough capacity figures. Yusick Ador answered that the ideal was seven projects per PE and requested congressional support for additional engineers. Tan also sought support for ongoing convergence projects, but Dizon deferred the matter to Congress while citing executive policies.
question: The committee was trying to establish whether DPWH had rationalized its project portfolio to match the capacity of its implementing offices and whether the 2027 budget should prioritize projects that could realistically be delivered. It also examined the effect of delayed releases, early procurement, ongoing-project funding, and convergence-program reforms on DPWH’s implementation capacity.
agency_position: DPWH said it was rationalizing projects to eliminate duplication, reduce small-ticket projects, focus on larger priorities, and bring project volume closer to the capacity of district and regional implementing offices. It acknowledged implementation constraints from late release of the 2026 capital outlay, sought additional engineers, committed to help identify priority and unfinished projects, and deferred the treatment and funding of ongoing convergence projects to Congress while complying with executive policies.
outcome: The committee received DPWH’s explanation of project rationalization and the stated implementing-office capacity benchmark, including seven projects per PE and the district-office example. The question of whether ongoing convergence projects would be funded, and the final allocation of projects among implementing offices, was left for congressional consideration and was not resolved in the exchange.

positions.position: Tan pressed DPWH to demonstrate that project volume was conservative relative to implementing-office capacity, asked for criteria and ballpark capacity figures, and advocated consideration and funding of ongoing projects.
Ador stated that the ideal capacity was seven projects per PE and said DPWH needed congressional help to secure additional engineers.
Dizon supported rationalization and prioritization but left further allocation and ongoing-project funding to Congress, subject to executive policies.

DPWH said its portal already carried roughly ten years of project records and supporting documents, but acknowledged that its existing summary followed district engineering offices rather than legislative districts. Bivensio Dizon committed to submit and publish the legislative-district NEP and supporting information, initially requested before the end of the meeting and later set by the chair for before 01:00. Rep. Janko also cited a flood-control example involving 900 million, 1 billion, and 100 million to show why phased project amounts should be disclosed. Dizon described multiyear appropriations as the policy direction for ongoing projects and agreed to follow the process for identifying congressional amendments or insertions. The chair clarified that the submission had to cover all legislative districts nationwide, but the transcript did not establish that delivery or publication had already occurred.

topic: Unfinished, ongoing, and delayed DPWH projects
summary: The DPWH presenter attributed slow 2026 procurement to the late release of roughly 460 billion in capital-outlay projects and reported 15,032 projects advertised and 7,467 awarded out of 17,764 projects. DPWH targeted 80% awards by the end of September 2026. Ian Amatong pressed for stronger project-engineer oversight, rapid completion of a hospital, and a policy prioritizing unfinished roads and other ongoing works; Bivensio Dizon agreed but said staffing and DBM rules constrained DPWH. Dizon said the department would seek additional engineer items and a possible exemption for continuing projects, and would provide an update on the Quezon Bridge. Dadah Kiram Ismula requested data on 50 ODA projects, commitment fees, and possible penalties, citing around 3,400,000,000 pesos in fees; DPWH undertook to submit the information. Mike Tan then questioned absorptive capacity, and DPWH reiterated the need for additional engineers and agreed to help identify unfinished projects. The issue landed with commitments for follow-up, while key policy and funding questions remained open.
question: The committee sought to establish why DPWH projects remained unfinished, delayed, or slow to be awarded and whether the department had sufficient implementation and supervisory capacity. Members also asked DPWH to prioritize ongoing works, complete hospitals and other unfinished projects, and account for delay-related commitment fees and other charges.
agency_position: DPWH attributed delays primarily to the late release of roughly 460,000,000,000 in 2026 capital-outlay projects and to limited project-engineer capacity. The department agreed that unfinished and ongoing projects should be prioritized, sought congressional help with DBM for additional engineers and possible exemptions for continuing projects, and undertook to submit project, bridge, ODA, and fee data.
outcome: DPWH acknowledged the delays and capacity constraints and agreed in principle that ongoing and unfinished projects should be prioritized. Several requested datasets and project updates were promised, but the DBM exemption, additional staffing, hospital completion schedule, and broader funding prioritization remained subject to further action.

positions.position: Unfinished hospitals, road links, and other ongoing projects should be completed promptly and prioritized in appropriations rather than repeatedly funded without completion. Project engineers should be physically present and accountable during implementation.

The committee needed a complete accounting of foreign-assisted projects, delays, commitment fees, penalties, and other lender charges because avoidable costs could have supported provincial health infrastructure.
DPWH should assess the absorptive capacity of each implementing office, assign projects according to technical capacity, and prioritize completion of unfinished and ongoing projects.
DPWH should improve preconstruction coordination with local officials and barangay captains before project implementation.

topic: Road widening and national road-system priorities
summary: Minority Leader Marcelino Libanan raised the proposed national road system, and Bivensio Dizon said DPWH was rationalizing widening toward the most dilapidated and priority sections. Libanan then pressed for a feasibility study for the Sorsogon–Northern Samar bridge, for which Dizon cited allocations of 120,000,000 and later 130,000,000, although the year-by-year breakdown was unclear. Dizon described the bridge as roughly 20 kilometers long, cited economic returns of 33% and 42%, and estimated six years for construction; he also committed to consider tourism in the evaluation. Representative Ian Amatong raised inadequate project-engineer coverage, citing an actual workload of one engineer for 30 projects against an ideal one-to-seven or one-to-10 ratio, and Dizon sought committee help for more DBM items. Amatong also sought faster hospital completion and prioritization of unfinished approach works, while Dizon agreed in principle and said DPWH would pursue a DBM exemption and prioritize ongoing projects. The chair additionally called for stronger preconstruction coordination, and Dizon agreed that such activities were critical.
question: The committee sought to establish how DPWH was prioritizing road widening within the proposed national road system and whether major inter-island links, particularly the Sorsogon–Northern Samar bridge, were feasible and adequately funded. It also examined whether project oversight, hospital construction, unfinished works, and preconstruction coordination were sufficient to ensure that district infrastructure priorities were delivered.
agency_position: DPWH said road widening should be rationalized and directed to the most dilapidated or otherwise priority sections rather than pursued indiscriminately. It supported a feasibility study for the Sorsogon–Northern Samar bridge, sought more project-engineer positions, agreed that unfinished works should be prioritized, and was willing to pursue a DBM exemption for continuing hospital projects, although funding and policy decisions remained partly outside DPWH's control.
outcome: DPWH committed to funding and advancing the Sorsogon–Northern Samar feasibility study, subject to subsequent funding and approval, and agreed to examine tourism considerations. Road-widening priorities were not contested after DPWH's explanation, but the hospital exemption, additional project-engineer items, and Quezon Bridge estimates remained dependent on DBM or later agency follow-up.

positions.position: He pressed for a feasibility study and a clear implementation and funding path for the Sorsogon–Northern Samar bridge, and supported advancing the project as a major national and regional link.

He called for stronger project-engineer supervision, rapid completion of the hospital in his district, a policy prioritizing unfinished works and approach roads, and more responsive district-level infrastructure delivery.
He directed attention to tourism in evaluating the bridge and urged DPWH to strengthen preconstruction coordination with local officials and barangay leaders.

topic: Sorsogon–Northern Samar and other major bridge projects
summary: Minority Leader Marcelino Libanan asked DPWH to establish the feasibility of the Sorsogon–Northern Samar bridge, including its economic return, timetable, and financing. Bivensio Dizon said the project was a critical Luzon–Visayas link and cited 120,000,000, later correcting or supplementing the figure with 130,000,000 for the feasibility study. He described the link as roughly 20 kilometers, cited a 42% economic rate of return, identified ADB, Korea, JICA, and AIIB as possible funders, and estimated six years for construction after feasibility and approvals. The Chair required tourism benefits to be considered in the evaluation, and the Secretary agreed. Rep. Ian Amatong and Rep. Mike Tan separately raised concerns about project-engineer workloads, technical assignment, absorptive capacity, and unfinished or ongoing projects; DPWH acknowledged the constraints and sought additional engineer items and continued coordination with Congress and DBM. The bridge feasibility commitment advanced, but financing, final approvals, and implementation remained unresolved.
question: The committee sought to establish the feasibility, economic return, financing, timetable, and technical implementation arrangements for the Sorsogon–Northern Samar bridge and other major bridge projects. Members also examined whether DPWH had enough project engineers and absorptive capacity to deliver technically demanding and ongoing bridge works.
agency_position: DPWH supported proceeding with the Sorsogon–Northern Samar feasibility study and considered the bridge a high-value Luzon–Visayas link with strong economic-return potential and possible external financing. The agency acknowledged serious project-engineer capacity constraints, sought additional DBM items, and said it would coordinate with Congress and other agencies on technically complex and ongoing projects.
outcome: The feasibility study for the Sorsogon–Northern Samar bridge was supported by DPWH, with funding figures stated and possible external financiers identified, but final financing, approvals, and construction remained prospective. The broader issues of engineer capacity, project assignment, and funding for ongoing bridge-related works were acknowledged and referred for further coordination with DBM and Congress.

summary: A majority member asked DPWH to provide the 2025 and 2026 school-building allocations for Regions 3, 4A, and 5 under the Basic Education Facilities Fund. topic: Asset preservation, road rehabilitation, and bridge maintenance
summary: Bivensio Dizon presented road-slip rehabilitation, drainage, safety barriers, aging bridges, flood mitigation, makeshift bridge replacement, and completion of unfinished buildings as asset-preservation priorities. He said many bridges were about 40 to 50 years old and that DPWH had often relied on savings because regular funding was insufficient. Rep. topic: Regional allocation equity and convergence priorities
summary: Bivensio Dizon presented DPWH's effort to shift regional allocations toward a more needs-based distribution, reducing Luzon's historical share from about 56% to roughly 52%, while raising the Visayas share to 20% and placing Mindanao at about 28%. He acknowledged that the distribution was not yet fully equitable and invited Congress to consider further reallocations, particularly for high-poverty regions. Dizon also said DPWH had reduced projects from a typical average of about 20,000 and the 2024–2025 level of about 25,000 by removing duplicates, emphasizing larger projects, and eliminating projects below 5,000,000 pesos under the VIP program. Representative Mike Tan questioned absorptive capacity, and DPWH answered that 80% of the 2026 program was expected to be awarded by the end of September; Yusick Ador gave an ideal capacity of seven projects per project engineer and requested help securing additional engineers. Tan later asked about ongoing convergence projects, including hospital and tourism-road works, and Dizon said their funding would be submitted to Congress subject to executive policies. The issue therefore produced agency commitments and explanations but left final reallocations and ongoing-project funding for congressional action.

topic: Hospital construction and interagency project coordination
summary: Rep. Ian Amatong raised concerns about absent project engineers, a delayed hospital in his district, and the need to finish unfinished works before starting new projects. Bivensio Dizon acknowledged that engineers were handling workloads as high as one to thirty projects against an ideal one-to-seven ratio and sought additional DBM items. Dizon said hospitals often fell under DOH budgets and that DPWH would seek flexibility for continuing hospital projects, while the chair called for stronger preconstruction coordination with local officials and barangays. Rep. Mike Tan then questioned DPWH's absorptive capacity, and Dizon projected 80% award of the 2026 program by the end of September. DPWH official Yusick Ador reiterated the ideal seven-project workload and requested more engineers. The agency agreed to help identify unfinished projects and said funding for ongoing convergence projects would be submitted to Congress, leaving DBM approvals and several project-specific matters open.

outcome: The agency agreed in principle with the members' calls for stronger preconstruction coordination, additional engineering capacity, and prioritization of unfinished and ongoing projects. Specific DBM approvals, additional staffing, the hospital completion timetable, and the status information on the Quezon Bridge remained subject to later action or submission.
